# Naive Voxel Geometry

Also called: Naive Voxel Rendering, Base Renderer Geometry

## Overview
Naive Voxel Geometry is a family of [object-order volume rendering](#10725-object-order-volume-rendering.md) techniques that represent scalar field data as explicit geometric primitives (typically cubes or quads) submitted to the graphics pipeline for rasterization [S1, S3, S4, unofficial][S2, unofficial]. It differs from [image-order ray-casting](#3161-image-order-ray-casting.md) by projecting geometry into screen space rather than sampling rays through the volume [G], and from optimized variants like [Sparse Voxel Rasterization](3032-sparse-voxel-rasterization.md) by generating primitives for all voxels without Level of Detail (LOD) reduction or greedy meshing, resulting in massive vertex counts for large scenes [S1, S4, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The family shares the fundamental mechanism of converting scalar field data into geometric primitives that are submitted to the graphics pipeline [G].

1. **Primitive Generation**: Each occupied voxel is represented by one or more geometric primitives. The most common representation is a cube (6 faces, 8 vertices for shared shading, or 24 vertices for flat shading) or a set of quads representing visible faces [G].
2. **Coordinate Transformation**: Voxel indices $(i, j, k)$ are transformed into [world space](#2511-voxel-coordinate-systems-and-conversion.md). For a dense grid with bounds $P_{min}$ and $P_{max}$ and dimension $N_{dim}$, the world position $P_{world}$ of a voxel center is calculated as:
$$
P_{world} = P_{min} + \frac{I_{voxel}}{N_{dim}} \times (P_{max} - P_{min})
$$
For unit voxels, this simplifies to $P_{world} = I_{voxel} \times V_{size}$, where $V_{size}$ is the voxel dimension [G].
3. **Rasterization**: The generated primitives are transformed into clip space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix and rasterized. Visibility is determined by the depth buffer (z-buffer) or a back-to-front painter's algorithm if transparency is required [G].
4. **Culling**: To manage performance, frustum culling is applied to exclude voxels outside the camera view. Back-face culling is often enabled to discard faces oriented away from the camera, calculated by the dot product of the view-space normal and the view vector [G].

## Subtopics

### [Naive Voxel Rendering](1103-naive-voxel-rendering.md)
Represents every occupied voxel in a dense grid as a full geometric cube and submits these primitives to the graphics pipeline for rasterization. It visualizes scalar field data by converting it directly into mesh geometry, differing from image-order ray-casting methods by projecting geometry into screen space rather than sampling rays through the volume [G]. Unlike optimized variants such as [Sparse Voxel Rasterization](3032-sparse-voxel-rasterization.md) or [SVO LOD Management](2990-svo-lod-management.md), this method generates primitives for all voxels without Level of Detail (LOD) reduction or greedy meshing, resulting in massive vertex counts for large scenes.

### [Base Renderer Geometry](3902-base-renderer-geometry.md)
Renders voxel data by converting occupied voxel indices into explicit geometric primitives (cubes, squares, or lines) and submitting them to the graphics pipeline for rasterization. It visualizes scalar field data by treating voxels as discrete 3D objects rather than volume textures [G]. It differs from [Voxel Fragment Shader Rendering](5849-voxel-fragment-shader-rendering.md) by generating geometry in CPU-side or vertex-shader-side buffers rather than computing ray-marching in the fragment shader, and from [Splatting and Point-based Rendering](4975-splatting-and-point-based-rendering.md) by using explicit polygonal faces instead of billboards [G].

### Cube Geometry for Volume Rendering
Generates explicit Vertex Array Objects (VAO) and Vertex Buffer Objects (VBO) for cube geometry [S1, unofficial]. The vertex layout uses a stride of 24 bytes per vertex, with Attribute 0 (Position) at offset 0 and Attribute 1 (TexCoords) at offset 12 bytes, both 3-component floats [S1, unofficial]. The index buffer uses 36 indices (uint32) to define 6 faces of a cube centered at the origin with size 2x2x2 (corners at +/-1) [S1, unofficial].

## Background
Originating from basic graphics programming tutorials and unofficial implementations, this approach serves as a foundational method for visualizing voxel data using standard rasterization pipelines [S1, unofficial]. It is commonly used in educational contexts, simple visualization tools, and as a baseline for comparing more advanced voxel rendering techniques [S1, unofficial].
